narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 67% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That does not mean you cannot succeed; it means the risk was high enough that admission was not offered.

The strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 2.80, it is below the 3.23 average among admitted students, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. The next most influential factor was your first-year academic standing: being in the third decile, compared with an admitted-student average of the sixth decile, also pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score of 40 was the third most important factor, and it actually helped your case because it is above the admitted average of 37.18, pushing toward passing. It was not enough to offset the weaker academic indicators.

Next, focus on strengthening the academic evidence. Consider additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program to show improved performance, especially in analytical writing and reading-intensive subjects. Meet with admissions or pre-law advisors about how to present your record, and apply to programs that review applications holistically. If you retake the LSAT, aim for a clear improvement; otherwise, use your above-average score as supporting evidence. Ask for feedback and consider applying after building a stronger recent academic record.
